By Isa Goldberg

December 16, 2025: Although not a memory play, memory itself plays a big role in Marjorie Prime, so does the ability to create a memorable experience, and in that way, strive for a sense of our own humanity.

At 85, Marjorie (June Squibb) appears to have dementia-related memory issues. The young man with her named Walter (Christopher Lowell) — after Marjorie’s husband, supplies her with historical information about their lives: how they met, the movies they liked…things like that.

At her age, the failure to remember things seems almost stereotypical. And more than a mere stereotype, the much younger man she converses with moves and speaks in a noticeably robotic fashion. In his not being entirely human, Marjorie notices some drawbacks. 

He’s a computer, programmed to converse with Marjorie and participate in her everyday life. Yet, his participation is limited to whatever data the computer has. Naturally, there is a broad band of disparity between the trained robot who pretends to be her husband, and the man, now deceased, with whom she had lived her life. 

With her husband, Marjorie created a shared universe that grew and extended their individual lives beyond just themselves. No longer able to do that, Marjorie opines on the flickering past, failing the capacity to envision, or achieve anything more. 

Living with her daughter, Tess (Cynthia Nixon) and her husband Jon (Danny Burstein), Marjorie feels alternately undermined, and grateful. Even in a conventional domestic drama these are not easy situations for families, and they’re not science fiction either.

As a family, which they are, the Primes are inhuman in the way they behave toward and reference one other. As we experience them, they are just like our own loved ones, with no more, nor less tactfulness and interest in others than the family we come home to.

Contrary to Happy Ending, last season’s robust, Tony-Award winning musical, in which two robots fall in love, and fulfill one another, robotic life appears more dissembling, in this new drama by Jordan Harrison. Here, it’s as if AI has taken over their lives.

As playwright, Harrison’s style of storytelling is most surprising. And this piece at the Hayes Theater is impressive, and compact with the story of three generations of Primes (one may assume), compressed into 85 minutes. 

Unfolding with multiple levels of meaning, Marjorie Prime is, on one hand, a play about how we deal with ageing and the aged. It’s not only how eager we are to throw them out, but how possessive we are of everything they’re supposed to leave us with when they finally go.

Most enjoyably, Harrison’s play is a humorous reflection on sentimentality in the theater. When at its most bourgeoise, it expresses ideas in a pretending, not truthful sort of way — like a robot that does not have the full picture, like Walter, say.

Ultimately, it’s about sentimentality itself, about being lost in a feeling of sadness that obscures logic. Ironically Walter, as a computer, is stuck in a sentimental world, because his existence is ebbed in the past, with no imagination for creating the future. It speaks to the way in which AI is taking over our lives.

“Science fiction is here, Jonathan… We buy these things that already know our moods and what we want for lunch even though we don’t know ourselves. And we listen to them, we do what we’re told.” Nixon’s Tess proclaims. 

As in Nixon’s Tony Award-winning role in Rabbit Hole, her Tess is a woman consumed with grief at domestic tragedy. And despite this play’s diversionary sci-fi quirks, the actress delivers a performance that morphs from elegant, to shameless, to alarmed. It’s one of her most believable roles yet.

Her immediate, instinctual chemistry with Burstein, pits the two stage titans in a marriage. In the way Burstein plays the role, it feels like he’s wearing a pair of old slippers. In fact, his role here is like a doppelganger to the son/memoirist he portrayed in the recent Broadway production, Pictures from Home. That, starring Nathan Lane and Zoë Wannamaker, along with Burstein, was indeed a sentimental send off to the boulevard comedy. 

In Prime, an ironic version of a family drama, the entire cast seems entirely at home. And none more than June Squibb, whose flawless, effortless portrayal of a there, yet-not-so-there, and all-seeing matriarch of the Primes is awesomely revealing. Just looking at her face, the audience in the play’s final moments is like facing the human cry, and it’s something we’ve seen all our lives!

That director Anne Kauffman brings this complex, tightly webbed drama to the stage with such clarity, and certainty speaks to her extraordinary aplomb. And that the entire set (Lee Jellinek) is green – the sofa is green, the wallpaper is green, does not entirely disparage the hope for new life, and growth, in spite of this apparent technology.

By Isa Goldberg

December 16, 2025: Although not a memory play, memory itself plays a big role in Marjorie Prime, so does the ability to create a memorable experience, and in that way, strive for a sense of our own humanity.

At 85, Marjorie (June Squibb) appears to have dementia-related memory issues. The young man with her named Walter (Christopher Lowell) — after Marjorie’s husband, supplies her with historical information about their lives: how they met, the movies they liked…things like that.

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

December 16, 2025: When Jordan Harrison’s Marjorie Prime premiered Off-Broadway at Playwrights Horizons in 2015, the play was hailed as a complex, compassionate rumination on grief and memory (I concurred.) It also was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize. Set in the near future, the short, powerful work focuses on the effects of advanced technology on a family facing aging and loss. 

Marjorie is in her 80s. She relies on an android programmed to resemble a younger version of her late husband Walter for company, comfort and to help fortify her fading memory. The presence of the living computer causes rifts in Marjorie’s relations with her prickly, depressed daughter Tess and her understanding son-in-law Jon. Familial tensions and tragedies follow as Marjorie, Tess and Jon all must come to terms with loss. 

Now a decade after the original NY production, a Broadway version presented by Second Stage at the Hayes Theater has an even deeper resonance. Artificial intelligence (AI) has arrived and the play is more immediate as the possibilities Harrison raises of duplicate departed loved ones come closer to reality. Memories become distorted when more palatable, idealized versions of the past are fed into the artificial beings’ software. For example, Marjorie and Walter’s proposal story is embellished from taking place after the couple went to the movies to see the silly comedy My Best Friend’s Wedding to the more romantic image of taking in the classic Casablanca at a charming indie theater. These distortions gradually become the accepted version as AI bots multiply and take over the flesh-and-blood characters’ shared narratives. Another theme becomes heartbreakingly clear as each member of the family must accept a death and turn to the AI-generated dopplegangers for consolation rather than facing the loved ones’ permanent absence. Harrison is examining our modern tendency to suppress our true emotions with fuzzy feel-good substitutes.  

Anne Kauffman repeats her directing chores from the 2015 production and delivers a subtly different, moving production, augmented by Daniel Kluger’s evocative original music. Lee Jellinek’s futuristic set perfectly blends the sterile scientific environment with subtle touches of a homey atmosphere. 

The cast skillfully balances raw emotions with the smooth, manufactured responses of the computer beings. Ninety-six-year-old June Squibb captures Marjorie’s wit and fiery passion to live as well as her frustration with her infirmities. She also keenly documents her struggle to retain her memories and the terrible acknowledgment that it’s a losing battle. Cynthia Nixon’s Tess is a maddeningly real amalgam of disappointed daughter, alienated mother of her own children and bundle of existential angst. She makes Tess’ obsessing over Marjorie’s well-being sympathetic and we can feel her ache of despair as she discovers the futility of advanced medicine and tech to stave off the inevitable. Danny Burstein is both lovably endearing and shatteringly intense as the aggrieved Jon who progresses from supportive comforter of his wife and mother-in-law to devastated survivor. Christopher Lowell as Walter has the difficult task of playing an artificial construct of a human. He conveys the computer’s desire to help and its emotionless demeanor. This is a thought-provoking and emotionally stirring production sure to ignite discussion and reflection on where we are as we hurtle towards an uncertain future where AI takes more and more from reality.

Second Stage’s other most recent production is equally multilayered and moving. Talene Monahon’s Meet the Cartozians (closed Off-Broadway at the Pershing Square Signature Center) follows an Armenian-American family’s legal battle to fit into Yankee society and the aftereffects of their struggle. The trauma of the 1915-6 Armenian genocide by the Turkish government still devastates the Cartozian clan as they face a challenge to their bid for citizenship in 1923 Portland, Oregon. Then, in the second act, 100 years later while waiting for an interview with a reality TV star (probably based on Kim Kardashian) in Glendale, California, four leaders of the Armenian-American community debate the status of their ethnic and cultural identity amid shifting political sensibilities.

Monahon raises many fascinating and complicated issues about race, religion, and the American Dream. “What is that makes a white person?,” one of the characters asks as the Cartozians navigate the treacherous intricacies of the immigration system with the aide of an Irish-American lawyer who has his own prejudices. The question recurs in the second act as the 21st century Armenian-Americans wrestle with the issue from a different angle. Are they white, Middle Eastern, or something else? Or are they just Armenian and what does that mean?

David Cromer delivers an understated, subtle staging with each of the six able cast members (Raffi Barsoumian, Will Brill, Andrea Martin, Nael Nacer, Susan Pourfar and Tamara Sevunts) giving equal weight to dual roles. Andrea Martin is shattering as the Cartozain matriarch and sharply funny as a contemporary activist tired of political correctness. Will Brill gives depth to the Irish-American lawyer and bite and humor to the reality-TV show techie. Tamara Sevunts skillfully portrays the intelligence of the maiden Cartozian daughter in the 1920s and makes her brief role of the Kardashian-like star more than a caricature. Raffia Barsoumian captures the vibrancy of the Cartozian eldest son and the insecurity of his contemporary counterpart who must deal with suspicion because of his Arabic appearance. Susan Pourfur passionately defends her character’s stand that Armenians deserve special census categorization while fussing over the state of the food she has prepared. Neal Nacer movingly limns the struggles of the Cartozian father to become a US citizen and a 21st century citizen seeking to understand his place in a changing America. 

Marjorie Prime ****

By Paulanne Simmons

December 8, 2025: We all remember the great dance scenes on Broadway and in movies, whether it’s Gene Kelly twirling around a lamppost in Singin’ in the Rain or Judy Garland following the Yellow Brick road with the Scarecrow, Tin Man and Cowardly Lion in The Wizard of Oz. But it took Nikki Feirt Atkins, producing Artistic Director of American Dance Machine for the 21st Century, to come up with the brilliant idea of putting all those iconic dance routines into a single show. The show is called Gotta Dance! and it’s running at The York Theater until December 28.         .

Co- directed by Atkins and Randy Skinner, Gotta Dance! features a talented cast of singers and dancers, who bring scenes from shows like West Side Story, A Chorus Line, Pippin, Singin’ in the Rain and Irving Berlin’s White Christmas to life with nothing more than a changing backdrop (scenic coordination is by Noah Glaister and projection design is by Brian Staton) and the accompaniment of a fantastic pit orchestra directed by Eugene Gwozdz.

Gotta Dance! pays tribute to the many choreographers who shaped Broadway and Hollywood, including Bob Fosse, Jerome Robbins, Gene Kelly, Michael Bennett, Susan Stroman and Billy Wilson. But the show also celebrates musical theater’s  most productive and prominent composers and lyricists: The Gershwins, Cy Coleman and Dorothey Field, Jule Styn and Stephen Sondheim, Stoller and Leiber, Leonard Bermstein, Irving Berlin.

There are scenes that are funny, serious or romantic. What they all have in common is their staging by heavy hitters like Donna McKeckmie, Robert LaFosse and Brian Lawton, and the brilliant execution of the performers.

Gotta Dance! is a show you gotta see.

By Samuel L. Leiter

December 4, 2025: In 1905, Jacob Adler, a giant of Manhattan’s Yiddish theater, spoke these (or similar) words from the stage of Teller’s Broadway Theatre in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg section: 

Ich bin a yeed. Hut den nit a yeed kyn oign? Hut den nisht a yeed kyn hent, kyn ayvurim, kyn kheeshim, kyn gefihln, kyn lydenshaftn? Genehrt mit der zelber shpys, geshedikt mit di zelbe vaffen, bafahlen fin di zelbe krenk, geheylt durkh di zelbe mittl, gevaremt un erkeltert fin dem zelben zimmer und vinter vi a krist?

This translation of Shylock’s most famous speech (“Hath not a Jew eyes?”) in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice is again being spoken, 120 years later, at another Brooklyn theater, the Polonsky Shakespeare Center across town. Adler played Shylock entirely in Yiddish as guest artist in an all-English-speaking stock company (Sidney Toler, later famous as a cinema Charlie Chan, was Bassanio). Canadian actor Saul Rubinek (Frasier and so much more), in a one-man play titled Playing Shylock, is the entire company (aside from an offstage stage manager’s voice), although only this speech is in Yiddish.

Mark  Leiren-Young’s play, first done as Shylock in 1996, has been revised several times so that Rubinek—who also contributed to the script—can impersonate himself in a metatheatrical performance. Directed by Martin Kinch, it imagines Rubinek to be playing Shylock in a production of Merchant that begins as if the second act is being delayed by tech problems. But, as the harried star frets, we learn from him that the show has been canceled because of community protestors complaining about its alleged antisemitism. Rubinek uses the opportunity to expand on various issues, not least of which is the supposed cancelation of The Merchant of Venice. 

Although he excoriates the decision, no such cancelation has ever been made (apart from a few shows padlocked in the 1920s on grounds of obscenity, or productions in school or community theaters). Some shows have been vehemently protested, of course, but the only significant cancelation Rubinek references is The Cradle Will Rock (1937), which wasn’t really canceled since it simply moved to another theater when the WPA closed the one it was playing at.

Even more questionable is the comment: “you can count the number of Jewish plays in New York on one hand. Maybe one finger.” I won’t bother to rebut it.

Other subjects touch on the play and the debate over the negative impact of its most prominent character, Shakespeare, Judaism, and Jewish actors. One section comparing Jewish law to Christian and Venetian law, spoken as if by Portia, is admittedly original, written, the actor says, in memory of a grandfather steeped in Torah law. 

Playing Shylock sometimes veers off topic, most egregiously when it supports the Oxford theory of Shakespearean authorship, claiming that Edward de Vere wrote the plays; even if that theory were valid (I know at least one brilliant theatre scholar who accepts it), it’s a distraction, and could save some time by being excised from a performance that, at 100 intermissionless minutes, eventually begins to drag, a feeling exacerbated by its ruminative, meandering structure. 

Much time is also devoted to Rubinek’s own interesting biography/identity as someone born to Polish Holocaust survivors (his dad was an actor who wanted to, but never did, play Shylock) in a Munich DP camp (1948), and raised in Canada, where he began acting at seven.

Playing Shylock, it should be noted, provides some historical background to The Merchant but is not a survey of how Shylock has been interpreted over the centuries, from redhaired and bearded comical villain (a tradition abandoned by Charles Macklin in the 18th century) to sympathetic victim (as per Henry Irving in the 19th century). Those interested in such history can find it in John Gross’s excellent Shylock: A Legend and Its Legacy.

Rubinek is dressed in the black hat, long black coat, yarmulke, and so forth, associated with Hasidic men, implying that the canceled production is in modern dress. His costume was designed by Shawn Kerwin, who is also responsible for the set, a thrust platform with a faux-marble floor pattern; the frame of a large crucifix hanging overhead and, for unexplained reasons, seriously distressed; a rear wall with a large crack in it; crudely painted side panels with “JEW” prominently displayed in graffiti style; a chair with red upholstery; and a long, wooden table. The functional lighting is by Jason Hand. 

Given how naturally Rubinek inhabits Shylock (when opportunities to speak his lines arise), it’s surprising that he never actually played the part in a full revival of The Merchant of Venice. He has the voice, the presence, the intensity, the insight, the emotion, and the ethnicity to make a memorable Shylock, although, at 77, he’s now perhaps a bit too old, considering the youth of Shylock’s daughter. 

Rubinek points out how few Jewish actors have played the role in major modern productions, while actors of different ethnicities, from black to Palestinian, have been cast in it. I myself have never seen anyone more powerful than the non-Jewish George C. Scott, back in 1963. Over the past four decades, the only Jewish Americans to play Shylock in New York were Dustin Hoffman (1989) and Richard Topol (2024), neither of them mentioned. 

Here and there, the star tosses off a joke as he wanders about the stage, his manner conversationally engaging and expressively honest, as if he were speaking extemporaneously. This can be problematic, though, as his tendency is to speak very fast, often seeming to mutter to himself under his breath, making many of his secondary lines inaudible.

Despite its several drawbacks, Playing Shylock is still worth a visit. It’s closing this weekend, however, so you’ll have to move quickly to squeeze it in.

Playing Shylock ****

By David Sheward

December 1, 2025: At this year’s Thanksgiving dinner, a young relative expressed her fears the world might be doomed because of AI and a certain lawless occupant of the White House. Us old folks had to reassure her that America and humankind in general has faced worst crises and we’ve come through, if only by the skin of our teeth or the seat of our pants. In similar conversations, friends have expressed the overwhelming fear that freedom and democracy are kaput in this country, that we are headed for becoming another Gilead (the fictional right-wing dystopia of Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale), and where can they safely emigrate to? 

These encounters brought home the realization that this is the perfect historic moment for Ethan Lipton’s The Seat of Our Pants (at the Public), a musical adaptation of The Skin of Our Teeth, Thornton Wilder’s crazy comedy of civilization triumphing over countless disasters. Debuting on Broadway in 1942, as America had just entered the Second World War, Wilder’s Pulitzer-Prize winning existential extravaganza imagines a typical modern suburban family, the Antrobuses standing in for all of humanity as they face glaciers, floods, and devastating wars. Characters speak directly to the audience, the fourth wall is broken numerous times, dinosaurs and mammoths romp through living rooms, and Noah’s Ark, the Ice Age and World War III are recreated. It’s insane but it works. As does Lipton’s adaptation which cleverly balances Wilder’s original, slightly dated script with modern sensibility and appropriately off-kilter, satiric songs. (John Kander, Fred Ebb, and Joseph Stein attempted their own musical version of Skin which went through regional productions, readings, and workshops, but never made it to New York.)

Lipton follows Wilder’s original fairly closely with a few well-placed detours into 2025 territory and his songs strike just the right note of whimsical earnestness. The Antrobus family and their maid Sabina are first seen in their New Jersey home struggling to stay warm as a sheet of ice threatens to obliterate mankind. As they gather around a diminishing fire with homeless refugees representing philosophical, religious and artistic figures, they sing “We were born out of the darkness/And should the darkness call us back/Let us pray we smell a brisket/As we slip into the black.” It’s that specific absurd image of a brisket that brings us into the Wilder mindset of bizarre comedy amidst terror. Director Leigh Silverman stages the goofy goings-on with a serious edge, allowing the comedy to subtly come through and the seriousness to slowly surface.

In the second act, we are in Atlantic City where Mr. Antrobus is president of a convention of mammals and a deluge of biblical proportions threatens to wipe us out again. Before the rains start, Antrobus’ happy home life is threatened by seductive beauty queen Sabina. In Wilder’s original, Sabina breaks character because a friend in the audience was similarly deserted by her husband. In Lipton’s update, Sabina interrupts her love duet with Antrobus to express her discomfort with the sexist aspects of the scene. This leads the entire cast to voice their objections and nearly lynch the narrator character who also is credited with writing the adaptation. The third act concludes with the family recovering from a titanic war, with the opposition led by the rebellious son Henry. The company then joins in choreographer Sunny Min-Sook Hitt’s dance of revitalization and renewal with Lipton’s ironically titled finale song “We’re a Disaster.” 

The veteran cast perfectly combines satire with investment in characters’ motives and objectives as well as putting over the enjoyable songs. Micaela Diamond is a hoot and a half as the mischievous, fickle Sabina and her spoiled-actress alter ego. Shuler Hensley captures Mr. Antrobus’ ambition to improve mankind’s lot and his flawed but caring paternal efforts. Ruthie Ann Miles conveys Mrs. Antrobus’ maternal love and wifely devotion as well as her steely determination to keep the home fires burning and the family fed. Damon Daunno is a fiery Henry, expressing his rage and insecurities while Amina Faye beautifully limns the hopeful pleas of the daughter Gladys as she progress from loving child to new mother after the war. Andy Grotelueschen makes a congenial narrator and Ally Bonino is a mysterious and sage Fortune Teller. 

Lee Jellinek’s versatile set and Kaye Voyce’s cartoonish costumes also set right combined tone of satire and seriousness for this quirky and endearing musical.

The Seat of Our Pants ****

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

November 30, 2025: A pair of two-character shows with differing depictions of amorous connections have recently opened on and Off-Broadway. One is a charming rom-com musical replete with cliches and plot-holes you could drive a truck through. Despite these flaws, Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) is an engaging and lighthearted romp, perfect for holiday fun. Strangers arrives on Broadway after runs in London and the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Mass. The other Off-Broadway offering, Rajiv Joseph’s Gruesome Playground Injuries, has no songs, is much darker, complex and more honest in its portrayal of the dysfunctional relationship of two accident-prone outsiders who come in and out of each others’ lives from elementary school to young adulthood.

The elaborately titled Two Strangers takes the basic romcom trope of two previously unacquainted, dissimilar characters meeting in a tense situation, running into conflict and then into each others’ arms. There’s shopping, sightseeing, sex, heartbreak, and an ambiguous resolution. Luckily, Jim Barne and Kit Buchan’s songs and dialogue are snappy and cute enough to overcome the overly familiar story arcs. Tim Jackson’s slick and smooth direction and choreography works perfectly on Sutra Gilmour’s versatile revolving set, employing set pieces in the shape of luggage of varying sizes to suggest multiple scenes in Gotham. 

Sam Tutty and Christiani Pitts are bubbly, bright, and multifaceted as the mismatched pair. Tutt exudes boyish enthusiasm and gleeful hopefulness as Dougal, a lonely British bachelor in New York for the first time to attend the wedding of his estranged dad. Pitts is the somewhat depressed Robin, the sister of the bride (much younger than the groom), who has been tasked with shepherding Dougal and performing a million ceremony-related chores including transport of the titular gateau from Flatbush, Brooklyn to Manhattan. Of course, Dougal’s puppyish eagerness and excitement for the Big Apple at first grates against Robin’s cynical veneer, but they eventually wind up canoodling. Several secrets involving ruptured family relationships for the two are gradually revealed, but too many loose threads are left dangling by the end of their brief time together. 

Several of Barne and Buchan’s songs, cutely staged by Jackson and endearingly performed by Tutty and Pitts, more than make up for these defects. “Under the Mistletoe” is a clever parody of countless Christmas duets from decades past, particularly Frank Loesser’s “Baby It’s Cold Outside,” featuring cringeworthy sexual elements. “American Express” is a fun frolic with Douglas and Robin rampaging through expensive shops, restaurants and hotels before crashing at the Plaza. “Dad” expresses Dougal’s fantasies about bonding with his distant parent and “What’ll It Be” chronicles Robin’s directionless  paths in love and life as she mechanically serves customers as a server at a coffee shop. The two actors beautifully balance comedy and pathos, displaying Dougal and Robin’s vulnerabilities and impressive pipes. There’s plenty to relish with these Two Strangers.

While Two Strangers follows a familiar amorous template, Rajiv Joseph (also currently represented Off-Broadway by Archduke) takes a decidedly non-romantic approach to the two-hander format with his Gruesome Playground Injuries, now in a bleakly funny revival at the Lucille Lortel, directed with equal attention to laughs and tears by Neil Pepe. Originally produced Off-Broadway by Second Stage in 2011, Joseph’s sharply observed script skips back and forth through time in the roller-coaster relationship between Dougie and Kayleen, chronicling their encounters after numerous accidents. Doug is more than accident prone, given to climbing telephone poles in rain storms, shooting off fireworks at close range, and riding his bicycle off the school roof. Kayleen smothers her insecurities with self-harm, indulging in cutting herself, alcoholism and meaningless sex. 

The pair come in and out of each other’s life, usually after serious injuries, and just miss connecting. From their first meeting in the nurse’s office in grade school, Doug believes Kayleen’s touch will heal him, but she resists his pleas for affection. 

Like the stars of Two Strangers, Playground’s two-person cast juggles outrageous humor with heartbreaking pathos. Nicholas Braun of Succession and two-time Tony winner Kara Young endow Doug and Kayleen with a vibrant physical life, throwing themselves around Arnuldo Maldonado’s stark hospital-like set making their numerous collisions and smash-ups totally creditable. Brian Strumwasser’s makeup design deserves mention for the realistic deception of their scars and bruises as do Sarah Lux’s costumes which suggest the different stages in the characters’ lives.. Young is especially moving as the damaged Kayleen, covering her soft center with a bristly exterior. Injuries is a sort of a reverse romantic comedy and a more devastating, but ultimately more honest experience than Two Strangers. 

Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) ***

By Paulanne Simmons

November 26, 2025: Samuel D. Hunter’s Little Bear Ridge Road has almost no set (Scott Pask) and not much by way of costumes (Jessica Pabst). One might think the writer, producers and director were determined to keep it a low-budget show, until an unnecessary actor (and expense) is introduced at the end. What the play lacks in other elements, it makes up in plots and subplots.

There is a dying aunt, a gay romance, a struggling writer, family trauma and existential angst. What else could anyone want? Perhaps a little coherence, focus and direction.

Ethan (Micah Stock) has come to his Aunt Sarah’s home in Troy, Idaho during the pandemic (he wears a face mask for a short while). His father has recently died, and Ethan wants to sell his home and settle some business affairs. His father, it turns out, was a meth addict, and terrible things apparently went on in Ethan’s  home, although we are not told exactly what. At one point the play seems to indicate his aunt helped out when he was young, at another point that she didn’t.

Anyway, that’s all water under the bridge (or should be) because Sarah (Laurie Metcalf) is dying of colon cancer. Ethan wants to help, but she is stubborn and independent. Ethan’s compassionate intentions are  complicated when he becomes evolved with a grad student named James (John Drea.) It all begins on a sex meet-up that turns into a date and ends up a long-term relationship.

Ther aunt gets very sick. The relationship doesn’t last. Ethan gets something published but we don’t know what and where. A sympathetic attendant (Meighan Gerachis) reads part of the story to Sarah and the play ends.

There’s lots of pathos here. How can we not feel bad for a guy who had a miserable childhood and now must deal with the death of his aunt, apparently the only relative he has left? How can we not sympathize with a woman who lives by herself and has no one to love or be loved by? But aside from Ethan’s awful childhood and Sarah’s cancer, there is little particularly engaging or unique about these characters. 

Laurie Metcalf is crusty and sharp-witted as usual. Director Joe Mantello may have just given her the script and let her do her thing. The two guys are earnest and awkward, as gay guys are so often portrayed onstage. They all spend most of their time watching television and hanging out on the couch (the lone piece of scenery).

Little Bear Ridge Road depends on our natural sympathy for people whose lives are messed up. So do soap operas.

By David Sheward

November 23, 2025: The big question is does the first Broadway revival of Chess solve the cult musical’s previously impossible problem of the messy book dragging down the magnificent, memorable score? The short answer is no, but it does provide powerhouse singer-actors (Aaron Tveit, Lea Michele, Nicholas Christopher, Hannah Cruz) the opportunity to display their impressive vocal chops and limning skills. Is it worth sitting through the Cuckoo-for-Coco-Puffs script to get to those compelling, stirring songs by Tim Rice and the Abba team of Benny Andersson and Bjorn Ulvaeus? That’s a matter of taste. It was rough going for me for the show’s nearly three-hour running time, but when the stars opened the mouths to vocalize, I forgot the melodramatic excesses and lame jokes in Danny Strong’s new book.

Chess is one of those shows that just won’t die. It began life as a 1984 concept album like Rice’s collaborations with Andrew Lloyd Webber, Jesus Christ Superstar and Evita. A fully-staged 1986 adaptation played London’s West End for three years, but a highly revised Broadway version closed after only two months in 1988. Ever since, the property has re-emerged in regional revivals, concerts, and recordings. The reason for Chess’s long game is the brilliant score. The sexy, catchy “One Night in Bangkok” was a Top 40 earworm. The sweet ache and passionate regret of “You and I” has always brought me to tears. “I Know Him So Well” is a tender duet expressing reflection over a failed love affair with gorgeous intertwining vocal lines. “Someone Else’s Story” is another beautiful ballad, heartbreaking in its simplicity.

The crazy story arc which contains these wonderful songs involves chess masters, affairs, the 1956 Soviet invasion of Hungary, the CIA, and the KGB. Plus this new version by Strong asks us to believe the fate of the entire world hangs on the chess matches—there are two of them, one for each act—with US and Soviet commanders poised to press the nuclear button depending on who emerges victorious. 

Strong has streamlined the crowded storyline (but not enough) and treats the material with a satiric, almost campy tone, with the Arbiter character transformed into a devilish narrator who constantly reminds us we’re watching “ a Cold War musical” and laying out the subtext in case we don’t get it. This narrator device removes us from the romantic-triangle aspects of the story and inserts contemporary groanworthy quips about RFK Jr. and his brainworm, Joseph Biden running for a second term, and just the mention of our current president (Tveit’s character name is Trumper, get it?). It doesn’t help that Bryce Pinkham, who has been a delight in previous musicals such as A Gentleman’s Guide to Love and Murder and Holiday Inn, delivers every line like a WWF ring announcer. He’s at full volume and intensity from his first entrance and has nowhere to go but over the top. Michael Mayer’s direction does flow smoothly with David Rockwell’s sleek, ultramodern set and Kevin Adams’ flashy lighting providing for swift, cinematic transitions. Mayer and choreographer Lorin Latarro also effectively employ a top-notch chorus to move the story along and provide background.

Luckily, we have a stellar line-up selling the score. Aaron Tveit captures Freddie Trumper’s narcissism masking his tortured vulnerability, particularly in “Pity the Child.” As Florence Vassy, his strategist and lover, Lea Michele delivers the goods on her ballads and conveys the character’s conflicting attractions between two chess champs. Nicholas Christopher emerges as a major Broadway star with his soaring interpretation of Anatoly Sergievsky, pouring his passion into “Anthem,” a declaration of love transcending borders. Hannah Cruz is most impressive as Svetlana, Anatoly’s Russian wife who emerges in the second act to reclaim her errant hubby from Florence. (Florence switches between Freddie and Anatoly.) Sean Allen Krill and Bradley Dean do their best to add resonance to a pair of stereotypical rival intelligence agents. 

The problem remains that the songs don’t connect strongly with the book. Hearing them on the original cast CD or as stand-alone solos evokes strong emotional responses, but the lyrics don’t always fit with the libretto. Too often the songs feel like generic ABBA hits. “Someone Else’s Story” was originally in the first act and has been pushed to the second to give Michele a 10 o’clock number, but here feels anticlimactic. In the battle between the book and the score, Chess still achieves a draw.

Just as Chess bangs us over the head by blatantly spelling out the authors’ intent, Nazareth Hassan’s Practice at Playwrights Horizons, tells us the theme rather than letting us figure it out for ourselves. Hassan is an intriguing playwriting talent. Practice offers a captivating look at power politics and manipulative behavior within an avant-garde theater company. But, as with their previous play Bowl EP, presented earlier this season at the Vineyard, the author spends too much time telling us what their play is about rather than showing us. In Bowl EP, Hassan profiled two rapper-skateboarders hiding their mutual attraction and damaged psyches with coded references to pop culture. Then a symbolic figure popped up and explained the resolution. 

Practice suffers from a similar tendency to explain for the audience. The first long act effectively details the dehumanizing efforts of dictatorial non-binary director Asa (a cunningly charismatic Ronald Peet) to bend his pliable young actors to his will. Each of the eager performers reveals embarrassing, dirty secrets which Asa unscrupulously incorporates in his performance piece. That process was intriguing, smartly directed by Keenan Tyler Oliphant, and performed with subtext and conflict by a proficient ensemble. (Karina Curet is particularly moving as a Chilean daughter of privilege fighting for her place in the company.) 

But the second act is Asa’s resultant theatrical work, clumsily labelled Self-Awareness Exercise 001, in which all of his manipulations and deceptions are laid out. Set designer Afsoon Pajoufar encloses the company in a glass cage and costume designers Brenda Abbandandolo and Karen Boyer dress them in post-apocalyptic rags. Though this (perhaps intentionally) pretentious and repetitive segment runs only 30 minutes, it felt like three hours. It’s unclear if Hassan is satirizing self-indulgent theater artists or if they want us to sympathize with Asa and their damaged acolytes. As with Chess, there’s an imbalance here. A smart, intriguing first act is pitted against a boring mess of a second act. This time the better act wins, but just barely.

title.rendered: Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) *****

content.rendered:
By Samuel L. Leiter

November 20, 2025: Two-hander musicals occupy the tiniest niche among the categories of Broadway musicals. A few more, like Marry Me a Little, to name just one, have played Off Broadway, but the Great White Way seems only to have seen I Do! I Do! (1966), The Story of My Life (2009), and The Last Five Years. The latter premiered Off Broadway in 2001 before finally receiving a revival on Broadway just this year.  Now, bringing a lightning shaft of unalloyed rom-com charm to Broadway’s Longacre Theatre is a smashing little British import called Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York), with book, music, and lyrics by Jim Barne and Kit Buchan, and direction by Tim Jackson. 

This four-layer confection—to extend the metaphor—is filled with mellow music, pungent performances, sweet staging, and velvety visuals. Originated at the Kiln Theatre in London before moving to the West End’s Criterion, it jumped the pond to play at the American Repertory Company in Cambridge, MA. It’s now on Broadway with one of its original young stars, Sam Tutty, giving a stunningly deft performance mingling hilarious comic chops with unexpected poignancy. It showcases not only his exceptional talents but those of American actress-singer Christiani Pitts (King Kong), whose career will hopefully skyrocket after this. 

According to the premise, Dougal (Tutty), 25, a goofy, wide-eyed, seemingly naïve, yet oddly perceptive and deceptively witty Brit, arrives at a New York airport and is Loony Tunes excited about being in the Big Apple for the first time. Waiting for him is Robin, 26, a lovely African American woman, sister of the woman Dougal’s much older father is about to marry. Dad abandoned his family before Dougal was born to make a fortune in America. Dougal and Robin: Opposites? Yes. Attraction? Give it time!

Dougal believes he’s been invited to the wedding by his dad, a fantasy version of whom lives in his deluded brain, father and son never having met; Robin knows better. The irrepressible bundle of joy that is the ginger-haired Dougal latches on to the notion that Robin is his “aunty,” which will be good for a big laugh.

Back home, Dougal lives with his mum and works at a local cinema, cleaning the place, selling candy, and being engrossed by the films he sees, an arrangement with which he’s perfectly content. Robin, from Brooklyn but living in Manhattan, is a no-nonsense, somewhat edgy, barista at a coffee shop, the Bump and Grind. She does all she can—albeit sometimes grudgingly—for her demanding older sister, especially regarding the forthcoming nuptials. 

Under sibling pressure, she agrees to go to Brooklyn to pick up the wedding cake. Despite her reluctance, Dougal attaches himself to her so he can squeeze as much sightseeing in during his 48 hours here. His overwhelming, movie-inspired fascination with the city she takes for granted gradually infects her; as Dougal’s child-like openness and honesty grows on her, Robin can’t help but succumb.

Thus begins the newly met couple’s dash around town (by subway, which thrills him), including a contretemps with the cake. They visit notable places, of course, and, with access to the father’s credit card, even spend an over-the-top night at the Plaza. Forced into such proximity, the pair can’t help but to learn more about each other—he even helping her find someone on Tinder—and to share emotional histories, with emphasis on Robin’s family issues (such as an estranged grandmother) and Dougal’s almost pathological obsession with a warped dream of his father. 

Gradually, the show, built on the classic boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl, boy leaves girl structure, builds to a touching emotional climax when the couple—with Dougal having to return home (“I’m only 4,000 miles away”)—sing “If I Believed” as snow falls all about them. Snow? In recent New York?

Two Strangers is filled with familiar rom-com tropes, yet it earns our love and respect because of the perfect way it forces you to believe in a romantic relationship between two people who you never in a thousand years would have believed would connect so quickly within a whirlwind 36-hour framework. It’s as artificial as AI yet as emotionally delicious as a slice of that cake they shlep around. Only one scene, where Dougal breaks down in tears, breaks the spell.

One of its strengths is how good the dialogue is when no one is singing; long, engrossing stretches go by as Robin and Dougal swap repartee, with the songs emerging from the dialogue almost naturally, telling the story and seeming an extension of the chatter rather than something separate. Robin has the closest thing to a traditional showstopper, “This Year,” late in the show, but that’s about the sole example of a number going in that direction.

The melodies are thoroughly listenable and relatable, being worth hearing again, their lyrics always clearly related to the characters and storytelling. Each song is as convincingly acted as sung. Both characters grow over the course of the show’s two hours and 15 minutes into people who clearly have gained from their journey across New York. As the icing on the cake, not only have they fallen in love with each other but we’ve fallen in love with them as well.  

Tim Jackson’s inventive staging is enhanced enormously by Soutra Gilmour’s truly clever set, placed on a turntable within a turntable, with its two mountains of silver-gray luggage suggesting at times the city’s skyline and, perhaps, a wedding cake. Having the luggage fitted with ribbons of light that can change color is a brilliant idea, and lighting designer Jack Knowles makes magic with it. Gilmour’s costumes are likewise fine, although they sometimes seem a bit too lightweight for the cold weather we hear so much about.

If Dougal and Robin can carry a cake across New York, you should be able to carry yourself across New York to see them do it. 

Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) *****

Running time: two hours and 15 mins. including intermission. twostrangersmusical.com

By Paulanne Simmons

November 20, 2025: The story of Oedipus has terrified and troubled people for generations. But it has never been more troubling and terrifying than in Robert Icke’s adaptation. There’s so much that Icke and his creative team got right, it’s hard to pinpoint exactly what turns this production into a masterpiece. But surely Lesley Manville’s portrayal of Jocasta is at the top of the list. 

Let’s start with the script, which alludes to Sophocles’ original play many times, but casts the plot in a new, modern and devastating light. 

Oedipus (a powerful Mark Strong) is not a king but a politician on the cusp of winning a major victory, with help from Creon (John Carroll Lynch) his brother-in-law and campaign manager. Oedipus’s sons Eteocles (Jordan Scowen) and Polyneices (James Wilbraham), and his daughter Antigone (Olivia Reis) bicker and tease each other much like spoiled college kids are wont to do. Most of all Jocasta is again a much older wife, but this time overwhelmingly attracted to her young and virile husband. The ultimate and inevitable tragedy is set. 

Of course we have already heard the horrifying predictions of Teiresias (Samuel Brewer) now a blind homeless man. Of course, Oedipus doesn’t believe him. And of course, we do. We know it’s just a matter of time before the shocking truth of his birth and all the rest is brought to light.

However, in this version, someone else is trying to warn Oedipus. His mother, who is really his stepmother, Merope (Anne Reid), has come all the way to Thebes to warn her son against looking for his birth certificate. Oedipus keeps putting her off in a condescending way that perhaps is a bit too brusque.

Hildegard Bechtler’s set puts us in a 20th century modern office with movable walls, fluorescent lighting (Natasha Chivers) and lots of windows. A digital clock sets the play in real time. And Tom Gibbons’ pulsing sound effects underline the drama and the threatening mood. Every time Oedipus dismisses his elderly stepmother, we cringe.

Icke does slip occasionally. There are times when the pace slows. Some scenes go on a tad too long. And certainly the coda that ends the show is anticlimactic and destroys the mood Icke has so meticulously created. But none of this can take away from the enormously powerful effect of this Oedipus. Surely when Manville delivers Jocasta’s searing revelations we are shaken to our very soul by her pain.

It’s hard to see Oedipus and not think of Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein, and their congressional enablers. But even if you don’t know the original play and don’t pay attention to the news, you’ll leave this Oedipus exactly as Sophocles wanted you to – wondering about the fate of humankind.

Oedipus **** 1/2

Running time: two hours, no intermission. oedipustheplay.com

By Samuel L. Leiter

November 19, 2025: The idea behind the new Off-Broadway musical, Reunions, at the New York City Center Stage II makes good sense. It takes two once very popular early 20th-century one-acts by very famous dramatists of the time, finds thematic and other links between them, and pairs them in an intermission-less, one hour and 40 minute sequence with the same ensemble in each. The results, while occasionally pleasant enough, are—with one or two exceptions—generally mediocre, both creatively and histrionically.

The first half of the program is adapted from Scottish playwright James M. Barrie’s “The Twelve-Pound Look,” which premiered in London in 1910. Its New York premiere was 1911, starring Ethel Barrymore, who later toured with it in vaudeville. The second half, a Spanish play (“Una Ardiente Mañana” or “Una Mañana de Sol”), by the Quintero brothers, Serafin Álvarez and Joaquín Álvarez, was first done in 1913; its New York debut, in a translation by Harley Granville Barker, waited until 1921, at the Neighborhood Playhouse, followed in 1929 by Eva Le Gallienne’s Civic Repertory Theatre, which offered a return engagement in 1930. In 1935, Le Gallienne brought it to Broadway for a single performance, as part of a repertory season.

If you didn’t spot the microscopic print at the bottom of the Playbill’s credits page, you’d never know that the script, although faithful to the originals, was by any other than book and lyrics writer Jeffrey Scharf; Jimmy Calire composed the music. Unfairly, despite the contributions of Barrie and the Quinteros, neither gets a bio, which is like Shaw not getting one in the Playbill for My Fair Lady.

Speaking of My Fair Lady, Reunions brings that show to mind in its use of the same Edwardian period (each playlet is set in 1910), its costumes (Jen Caprio) and coiffures (J. Jared Janas) serving only to remind you of how second-rate most of this show’s score is in comparison to the brilliant one of Lerner and Loewe. A small onstage orchestra (piano, bass, guitar/cello, percussion), part of it offstage to either upstage corner of the set, is supplemented in each play by the unnecessary trope of having one or two onstage, stone-faced, costumed musicians (Janet Aldrich and Pearl Rhein) playing guitar or violin to help highlight the action.

Both plays use the same basic set of a thrust stage, by Edward Pierce, backed by a large, framed landscape painting whose image of a tree extends onto the backdrop behind it. A colorful revolving disc is set into the floor to provide visual variety when it readjusts stage positions. Furnishings are limited, mainly a desk and chair in Barrie, and a park bench in Quintero.

“The Twelve-Pound Look,” which has a proto-feminist plot, presents Harry Sims (Bryan Fenkart), a smug, wealthy man overjoyed at the imminence of his being knighted. With the assistance of his guileless wife, the future Lady Emily (Courtney Reed), bedecked in the diamonds she plans to wear, he keeps practicing the moves he’ll make when the monarch dubs him “Sir.” Overwhelmed by congratulatory letters, he hires a typist, Kate (Chilina Kennedy), to respond to them. She, unaware of who has hired her, turns out to be his first wife, who left their oppressive marriage, in which she, like her successor, was little more than decoration. Secretly saving the eponymous sum so she could buy a typewriter, she learned to type so she could become independent and earn a living without Harry, a choice his present wife begins to ponder for herself. 

“A Sunny Morning,” set in a Madrid park, is a romantic comedy involving a pair of geriatrics, reminiscent of the scene in the show and movie, Gigi, in which a pair of former lovers (in the film Hermione Gingold and Maurice Chevalier) comically meet again to stumble comically through their memories of their long-past liaisons. Here we have Don Gonzalo (Chip Zien) and Dona Laura (Joanna Glushak), once passionate, now elderly. She, elegant and refined, feeds pigeons to pass the time. The irritable old Gonzalo encounters her, and their discourse at first is laced with sarcasm. But they become more amenable after a pinch of snuff causes such sneezes that it clears their heads (his sequence of ever louder blasts is intended to be hilarious; it’s not). Gradually, as they idealize their past selves, their mutual past becomes clear, their attitudes toward one another shift, and hints of rekindled romance begin to flutter.

The material is pleasant enough in the abstract, a diversion from the provocative subject matter and language of much modern drama, and the show might have had a chance with more memorable music. But, aside from one or two tuneful, rhythmically appealing numbers in “A Sunny Morning,” the abundantly stocked score (22 numbers are listed for the two halves) is unimpressively bland. 

Gabriel Barre’s uninspired direction and choreography also leave much to be desired, and his casting wins no prizes. While Kennedy and Reed are passable as the women in “The Twelve-Pound Look,” Fenkart is out of his depth as the snooty British social climber and marital misogynist, especially when he tries to be funny. He’s also outclassed in the singing department by his costars. In “A Sunny Morning,” Glushak holds her own quite nicely, but Zien is hard to swallow as her superannuated former lover. A popular actor who has contributed much to New York theatre, he lacks the romantic charisma even the elderly Gonzalo requires.

These two comedies of manners are satisfactory partners, each dealing in a compact way with meetings between genteel people who, after many years apart, recall their romantic pasts together. In one, a woman has outgrown her former husband, in the other a couple finds it difficult to revisit their unhappiness. Memory and regret, self-knowledge included, bind the plays, as does their reliance on duet scenes between Kate and Harry, and Donna Laura and Gonzalo. 

For all its seemingly clever concept and the nostalgic charm of its source material, Reunions ultimately stumbles under the weight of its own mediocrity. The adapted plays, though inherently appealing, are undermined by a forgettable score, tepid staging, and performances that, with one or two exceptions, rarely rise above the serviceable. What should have been an inventive pairing of two graceful, century-old comedies instead feels dutiful and uninspired, its opportunities for wit, lyricism, and emotional resonance squandered by bland music, flat direction, and misjudged casting. 

By the end of its one hour and 40 minutes, Reunions proves less a celebration of theatrical rediscovery than a reminder of how easily good ideas can falter when not matched by execution worthy of their promise.

Reunions ** 1/2

By David Sheward

November 19, 2025: The countdown clock in Hildegard Bechtler’s sterile set for Robert Icke’s explosively dramatic adaptation of Sophocles’ Oedipus was ticking down to the final minutes and I was having trouble breathing. Even though the shattering conclusion of incest and destruction is well known to the civilized world, Icke’s modern version of the classic Greek tragedy is so perfectly paced and infused with such suspense, the tension was palpable. The prideful Oedipus (a dynamic Mark Strong) is about to find out his true identity. The revelation will destroy his burgeoning political career, his family, his very essence, and erase his hubristic pride. The next few moments are a stunning coup de theater in the Broadway season’s most stunning dramatic presentation.

Now at Studio 54, produced in association with Roundabout Theater Company after an Olivier Award-winning run in London, Oedipus is everything theater should be—thought-provoking, emotionally stirring and empathy-evoking. Icke’s adaptation is smart, relevant and eloquently addresses issues afflicting our contemporary body politic. His direction is flawless, skillfully and slowly building the anxiety till the inexorable finale. The placement of that large clock marking the minutes and seconds to the end, and Tom Gibbons’ eerie sound design add to the stress. Strong and Lesley Manville, painstakingly documenting the gradual crumbling of the colossal egos of Oedipus and his wife Jocasta, lead a magnificent cast, each clearly delineating their part in the hero’s downfall and their reactions.  

Icke whose previous transatlantic triumphs have included a masterful Hamlet and Oresteia as well as an updated version of an obscure Arthur Schnitzler play called The Doctor, has transformed Oedipus from an ancient Greek king into a 2025 progressive political candidate on the cusp of winning an decisive elective victory. We open with a giant video screen (Tal Yarden designed the CNN-style videos) depicting Oedipus’ campaign vows to reform a corrupt government, sounding much like NYC mayor-elect Zohran Mamdani, and promising to release his birth certificate, recalling Barack Obama.  

The screen raises and we are in campaign headquarters as the election results are pouring in. Oedipus’ mother Merope (stern and mysterious Anne Reid) urgently requests private time with her son. (We all know where that’s headed.) Meanwhile, Oedipus receives ominous warnings from the blind seer Teiresias (intense Samuel Brewer) that he will murder his father and sleep with his mother. As the protagonist attempts to ferret out the meaning of this riddle, we learn this contemporary Oedipus wants to reform the future. Strong makes Oedipus a complex figure. He revels in the hero’s robust ambitions, but also exposes his tender side. Oedipus compassionately accepts a gay son, promises better living conditions for his constituents, and loves his family. But Icke stresses Sophocles’ theme that the past can determine destiny. 

And Manville is just as complicated. She is a driven political force, but also deeply damaged. In a searing monologue, she achingly reveals Jocasta’s trauma at the hands of her first husband the previous ruler, Laius. There is also a sizzling sexual connection between Oedipus and Jocasta, which leads to their undoing. 

In addition to those already cited in the supporting cast, there’s admirable from John Carroll Lynch’s cautious Creon, the advisor who believes in following the rules at all costs; Teagle F. Bougere as a haunted witness to Oedipus’ deeply-held secret; Bhaskar Patel’s faithful family retainer; and Olivia Reis, Jordan Scowen, and James Wilbraham as Oedipus’ loving adult children, each with depths of their own. 

Though the story is more than 2,000 years old, Icke and his company have brought Oedipus into the 21st century, alive and 

Roundabout is presenting another multilayered political drama (but it’s really a comedy), Rajiv Joseph’s Archduke at their Off-Broadway space, the Laura Pels. As in his previous works such as Guards at the Taj and Describe the Night, Joseph depicts ordinary figures caught up in the tidal wave of history. Here three clueless teenagers, each with a fatal diagnosis of tuberculosis, are recruited to assassinate Archduke Ferdinand in 1914 Sarajevo, setting off World War I. None of them really understand the geopolitical machinations behind their actions, they just want their young lives to have some purpose before they are snuffed out by disease, and to find a really good sandwich.   

Joseph sharply satirizes patriotic fervor and nationalistic honor with the scheme’s ruthless recruiter, Dragutin “Apis” Dimitrijevic, referred to as “The Captain,” played with gravelly gusto by Patrick Page. He plies the starving boys with a lavish meal, presented by his eccentric cook (Kristine Nielsen, riotously funny as always), and regales them with bloodthirsty tales of heroism to get them to sign up for certain death. Dark humor vies with existential dread as the young men struggle to understand their destiny and finally yearn for the simple pleasures of life—finding love, raising a family, enjoying a sandwich. Director Darko Tresnjak perfectly balances the conflicting strains of comedy and tragedy. 

Jake Berne, Adrien Rolet and Jason Sanchez capture the young fools’ confusion and yearning for meaning in a seemingly meaningless universe. Page adeptly reveals the Captain’s ferocious, blind devotion to duty and Nielsen is a merry buffoon and frightening mother figure with hidden layers she slowly peels back. Archduke is a bizarre Beckett-like farce with the clowns crying in the darkness, howling against the tides of history.

Stephen Hamilton brings a stylish thought- provoking staging of Bradbury’s 1953 science fiction classic to Bay Street Theater in Sag Harbor.

By Patrick Christiano

November 18, 2025: Stephen Hamilton’s stylish production of Bradbury’s dystopian novel about a future society where books are outlawed and firefighters burn any that are found is more urgently relevant today than ever. The story follows Guy Montag, played by John Kroft, a firefighter who begins to question his part in the burning of books after meeting a free-spirited young woman, Clarisse, played by Anna Francesca Schiavoni. The novel explores themes of censorship, complacency, and the dangers of mass media. Hamilton’s streamlined adrenaline-charged staging runs a brisk 90 minutes and emphasizes the throughline of the story, the importance of knowledge and individual thought.

Hamilton has incorporated visual and sound effects to bring the story to life with the assistance of Mike Billings’s outstanding scenic and projection design along with a strong cast. The result is thrilling and unsettling evening which draws parallels to our current political climate in increasingly frightening fashion.

The powerful drama follows the inner struggle of Guy Montag, a civil servant living in a future world where books are outlawed. However, when Montag meets Clarisse, she becomes a catalyst with many different thoughts and ideas. She asks him many questions, and he begins to think about what he has been doing and soon finds himself in a risky and highly explosive situation. 

Now he must choose between what he has been doing or risking everything for the right to think.

The title Fahrenheit 451 refers to the temperature at which paper ignites. The Bay Street Theater production is part of their Literature Live series and mirrors our current fractured society beautifully, even more than during the McCarthy era, which inspired Bradbury to write the novel. Bradbury wrote, “We need not to be let alone. We need to be really bothered once in a while.”

A special treat are the cameo appearances of Broadway producers Bonnie Comley and Stewart F. Lane in the video projections and live on stage at the play’s end, where it may be difficult to recognize them

The book has been adapted across many mediums, including two motion pictures, as well as multiple stage versions, including a 2006 Off-Broadway mounting at 59E59 Theaters.  A new Broadway -bound production is in development with a script by Pulitzer Prize winning playwright by Martyna Majok. Now is the chance to be ahead of the curve. Don’t wait, see Hamilton’s exciting staging of Fahrenheit 451 now.

title.rendered: The Queen of Versailles ***, The Baker’s Wife ****

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

November 17, 2025: Stephen Schwartz has the distinction of having three shows running simultaneously on New York stages. In addition to the long-running Wicked, Schwartz’s songs are on display in The Queen of Versailles, a new musical based on the documentary film about socialite Jackie Siegel’s quest to build the largest private home in America, and The Baker’s Wife, based on Marcel Pagnol’s film, which closed during out-of-town try-outs before reaching Broadway in 1976. Both scores serve their respective shows well. But the former is a mixed bag of confused storytelling choices and Broadway excess while the latter is an intimate, delightful Off-Broadway charmer.

There are many satisfying elements in Queen of Versailles, not the least of which is Kristin Chenoweth’s magnetic star performance as well as Michael Arden’s fluid, fast-paced direction and Dane Laffrey’s elaborate scenery and clever video design, combining elements of campy bad taste and European chic. The same can be said for Christian Cowan’s century-tripping costumes. But it’s unclear how Schwartz and book-writer Lindsey Ferrentino want us to feel about Chenoweth’s character, the vapid but tenacious Siegel. We learn plenty about her driven struggle to rise above the middle-class status of her hard-working parents (solid Broadway vets Stephen DeRosa and Isabel Keating). She works several jobs in high school, gets an engineering degree and survives an abusive first marriage. But her goals and means of achieving them are questionable at best. 

After marrying the decades-older, fabulously wealthy Time Share King David Siegel (F. Murray Abraham, doing his best with a thankless role) and going on a honeymoon in France, Jackie decides to replicate the extravagant Palace at Versailles in her hometown of Orlando, Florida. Why? “Because We Can” she and the company sing in a number celebrating unrestrained consumption. Louis XIV (Pablo David Laucerica) and Marie Antoinette (Cassondra James)—both exhibit lovely voices, BTW—pop up in parallel-time scenes, meant to demonstrate what? That Jackie and David are just as bad as the French aristocracy who ended up guillotined by starving revolutionaries? (Jackie buys an actual guillotine without irony.) But then are we also supposed to admire Jackie’s pluck and determination while simultaneously disdaining her boundless avarice and materialism? 

Despite the mixed signals, Schwartz’s songs are varied, funny and appealing and there is wit in Ferrentino’s book. There are poignant moments provided for Jackie’s sensitive, misfit daughter Victoria, seeking to break away from her mom’s obsessive acquisitiveness. Nita White feelingly delivers a heartbreaking ballad “Pretty Wins” detailing Victoria’s alienation from conventional notions of beauty. Tatum Grace Hopkins as Jackie’s orphaned niece Jonquil also chronicles a moving emotional journey, traveling from mimicking her aunt’s greed (the funny “I Could Get Used to This”) to independence and self-sufficiency. As David’s son Gary who also works for him, Greg Hildreth exposes the psychic damage rendered by his dad’s coldness. Melody Butiu conveys the loneliness of Sofia, the family nanny who has not seen her real family in the Philippines for years. 

But the star of the evening is Chenoweth who captures Jackie’s sparkling wit as well as her clueless avarice, re-establishing her status of the Queen of Broadway. Too bad Queen of Versailles is so confusing and doesn’t delve very deeply into the issues of shallow American consumerism it raises.

Whereas Queen of Versailles documents over-the-top culture in both content and execution, The Baker’s Wife sets its sights on a much smaller level and achieves more. The original production struggled out of town for six months, replacing its leads Topol and Carole Demas with Paul Sorvino and Patti LuPone before finally closing in Washington DC without ever reaching Broadway. The show has since attained cult status with numerous productions in regional theaters, London, and Off-Broadway and one of Schwartz’s songs “Meadowlark” has become a popular choice for auditions and cabaret acts. Gordon Greenberg has staged many of these versions and his current incarnation at Classic Stage Company does not completely cover up the show’s flaws, but it does take full advantage of its high points. A cast full of experienced Broadway and Off-Broadway players gives full life to the slight story by the late Joseph Stein and Schwartz’s flavorful score.

Pagnol’s 1938 film, based on a chapter in Jean Giono’s 1932 novel Blue Boy, is a thin but enchanting tale concerning a small-town baker who sinks into depression and ceases making bread when his much younger wife deserts him for a handsome stud. The village, desperate for their daily supply of baguettes, unites to retrieve her. She finally realizes her younger lover can only fulfill her sexual urges but not her emotional needs and she returns. That’s it. Stein’s book stretches out the story and Schwartz supplies some extraneous musical numbers. 

Fortunately, the cast fleshes out the many colorful characters of the village and Greenberg and set designer Jason Sherwood transform the CSC space into a believable, rustic environment inhabited by credible residents. As the baker and his errant spouse, Scott Bakula and Ariana DeBose have chemistry and spark. DeBose beautifully lands “Meadowlark,” the highlight of the show in which the baker’s wife expresses her inner conflict between passion and affection. DeBose and Kevin William Paul as her lover also exhibit Stephanie Klemons’ eloquent choreography. My only quibble with Bakula’s casting as the mature baker is he is still ruggedly handsome and trim, so there is less of a contrast between him and his romantic rival. 

Judy Kuhn is delightfully wise as the cafe owner’s wife and sort-of narrator. As the town teacher, Arnie Burton manages to get laughs with small gestures. Even a simple thing like removing his glasses gets giggles. Nathan Lee Graham is salaciously slinky as the lascivious Marquis who keeps a retinue of “nieces.” Robert Cucciolo, Alma Cuervo, Kevin Del Aguila, Manu Narayan, Sally Murphy, and Will Roland all have moments to shine in this amiable curio. Between the mansion of Versailles and this intimate French village, I’ll take the latter.

title.rendered: Rob Lake Magic with Special Guests The Muppets **

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

November 14, 2025: “Now this show has some real star power,” declares Miss Piggy, the porcine puppet star, late in Rob Lake Magic with Special Guests The Muppets, now in an abbreviated run at the Broadhurst. The glamorous felt pig is not wrong. The family-friendly special attraction does feature some fun-filled fare for the kiddies, but lacks a strong driving force. Lake himself, who gained recognition as a finalist on America’s Got Talent, is a genial enough presence, attractive and self-effacing, but his demeanor is so mellow and laid-back, his impressive illusions produce mild smiles rather than astonished gasps. Unfortunately, the show has not sold enough tickets to justify its original limited holiday-season run and, after delaying the official opening twice, producers have decided to shutter after only four performances and 15 previews. 

There could be several reasons for this disappointing box-office performance. The high price of Broadway ducats may have kept families with multiple children away. In addition, the similar Jamie Allan’s Amaze! is still running Off-Broadway at New World Stages until Feb. 22 and parents may have opted for the more affordable and intimate alternative. Lake’s efforts suffer by comparison with Allan’s not just in the economy department. Allan’s venture had a narrative arc and structure, offering details on his childhood obsession with legerdemain, his parents’ show-biz credentials as well as the history of magic in vaudeville and popular entertainment. In short, we get to know Allan as a person, not just as a performer. Lake briefly touches on his background, but we are not offered similar insights into his development as a magician. In addition, several of the illusions in both shows are similar.

The program credits do not list a director or writer. Lake created and conceived the evening. Bethany Pettigrew is down as “Creative Consultant” and Kevin J. Zak is credited with “Additional Material.” Perhaps a stronger creative hand behind the scenes would have crafted the show into a cohesive whole. As it stands, the illusions do not feel connected and the usually delightful Muppets seem like cameo performers. Kermit the Frog, Fozzie Bear, Rowlf the Dog, Gonzo the Great and Animal the drummer appear early in a taxicab, exchanging slightly amusing banter with Lake. Fuzzy later shows up in a box, delivering elementary-school level gags. It’s significant that Miss Piggy does not show up until much later and her campy, imperial tone is much missed. I did enjoy Gonzo’s quips about the supposedly upper-class Broadway audience as he prepared to be shot out of a canon. “Good evening, Cultural Elite! Here’s a trick you can tell your butlers about!” he cries in the one of the show’s few instances of adult humor.

There is also a guest shot with a current Broadway performer helping out with a pick-a-card trick. Jak Malone of Operation Mincemeat was the celebrity at the performance attended. Audience members are also called upon to ascend the stage to assist in the proceedings and it must be a thrill for them, each seemed genuinely astonished at Lake’s efforts, enhanced by assistants videoing their reactions. Jessica Forcha, Jennifer Orf and Natalie Vatalaro are sexy and vibrant stage assistants. 

Even given the show’s weaknesses, this is a cute distraction for families wishing to expose their children to Broadway. Too bad it will disappear so soon.

content.rendered:
By Isa Goldberg

November 13, 2025: Illusionist Rob Lake does magic on Broadway. Not any ordinary Svengali, Lake is charismatic, and confidently narcissistic. Pretty hot, in a tee shirt and black leather pants, he starts out with the most obvious tricks, like sawing a woman in half.

But his sleight of hand is quick, and no one seems to notice that these are old tricks we’ve seen a million times. Outgoing, fetching, and somewhat flamboyant, he catches the audience off guard.

Early on he promises us is that he ”will influence everyone in this audience” with his mind. But what he really calls on is more classically, the ability to suspend our disbelief, and he is quite good at that. 

In an act that is almost insanely convincing, Lake asks three audience members for their wedding rings. One he pulls right off a guy’s finger without leaving the stage, followed by his videographer who projects this trick so we can watch it close-up. Pulling one ring through another, literally passing one gold band through another and another, he seamlessly links three rings.

Metaphysically speaking, this Magician can break through the molecular structure of gold, bypassing the fact that two things can never be in the same place at the same time. With focused concentration, and a powerful will, man can do this, and in showing us the way, Lake weds himself to the audience. 

Fortunately, he finds guests to crash his act before we can. The Muppets’ Miss Piggy is one of the crown jewels he breaks out with, and Tony Award winning Annaleigh Ashford, the real person, emerges from the audience, which is weird because at this moment she looks entirely different from any of the awesome, quirky, ridiculous, warm, endearing characters she’s played on Broadway.

In this smorgasbord of entertainment, Lake performs a Vegas-style act evoking the Liberace effect of Sigfried and Roy. Here the waterfall, and faux Greek statues frame his awesome physique as he stands over a woman whom he levitates. Floating on air, in her lavender flowing gown, there are no strings attached. Only the heat of this godlike man can explain the way she swells up in the air and gracefully glides down.  Accompanied by swirling romantic music, it’s so outré, it leaves no question at all.

Later acts, especially one in which he walks into the audience, grabs a lobby bar napkin from someone sitting nearby, and engages an attractive woman in conversation, and while twisting the napkin, he suddenly transforms it into a beautiful red rose. While you may not find this one explained in a YouTube video, it’s overtness and similarities to acts like pulling a rabbit out of a hat, kind of casts a shadow of doubt on how likely metal passes through metal, or women levitate 10 feet in the air. 

As overkill, it’s intentioned, as if he were breaking the fourth wall, and confronting us with the impalpable nature of illusion. The grand illusion, of course comes at the end with Lake, mounted on his red motorcycle, triumphant, projected on a video screen.

The videography (Kate Ducey), as executed by Lake’s assistants is quite erotic, while Nick Solyom’s lighting is as camp for the Vegas style scenes, as it is bright for the sleight of hand tricks. 

It’s actually a fun experience, and hanging out with families (especially when they’re not yours) is enjoyable. Later in the show, Lake introduces his understated side in a scene with a boy from the audience who he introduces to a book, which is full of its own magic.
